site.name: The Cloister Museum of Sacred Glass & Stone
site.concept: A museum of high medieval cathedral arts — stained glass, illuminated manuscripts, and architectural fragments from the great cathedral-building age of northern France.

card_pattern: Each artifact, gallery, or program is presented inside a tall pointed-arch frame the height of roughly two body columns, with a gold-leaf hairline border and a small quatrefoil cusp at the apex. Card titles set in Cinzel Decorative small-caps in gold-leaf; metadata (date, provenance, accession number) sits below in a single column of EB Garamond italic; the body description begins with an illuminated drop cap in madder red on a cobalt panel. Section breaks within a card use a single inline vine-leaf ornament between paragraphs.
design_rules: The site reads as cathedral interior — saturated cobalt walls, gold-leaf ornament concentrated only at structural transitions (heads of arches, capital bands, footer arcades), and tall narrow text columns that mimic lancet windows. Pointed arches and quatrefoils are the only frame shapes permitted; round arches and pastel tints are forbidden. Ornament is high-density at edges and corners, but body fields stay quiet so the jewel-tone glass and illuminated capitals carry the eye.

pages.title: The Cloister Museum of Sacred Glass & Stone
pages.content_brief: Hero introduces the Cloister Museum with a rose-window centerpiece beneath a tall pointed-arch silhouette, framing the institutional motto 'Lux perpetua luceat — let perpetual light shine.' Three featured exhibitions: 'The Cobalt of Chartres: Glass from the Western Workshops, 1194–1235'; 'Ribs and Buttresses: Drawings of the Master Masons of Reims'; and a manuscript loan, 'Folios from the Très Riches Heures.' A short paragraph from the director, Mère Geneviève d'Argenteuil, welcomes visitors to the new wing opened in the feast-month of Michaelmas, 2024.

pages.title: Galleries & Permanent Collection — The Cloister Museum
pages.content_brief: An itemized walk through the seven permanent galleries: the Lancet Hall (24 panels of 13th-c. French stained glass, on long-term loan from the Diocese of Soissons); the Tympanum Court (carved Last Judgment fragment, Amiens workshop, c. 1245); the Scriptorium (12 illuminated leaves under low light, including a Beatus initial from the Abbey of Saint-Sever); the Reliquary Chamber; the Capitals Cloister; the Rose Window Study; and the Mason's Yard. Each gallery entry gives accession numbers, provenance, and conservation notes.

pages.title: Current Exhibitions — The Cloister Museum
pages.content_brief: Three temporary exhibitions on view through Candlemas, 2 February 2025. 'The Cobalt of Chartres' examines pigment chemistry of the famed bleu de Chartres, with side-by-side panels from the Belle Verrière. 'Hand of the Master: The Reims Sketchbooks' presents 38 silverpoint drawings attributed to the workshop of Villard de Honnecourt. 'Gold and Lapis: A Book of Hours from Bourges' displays a private-collection manuscript open to the Annunciation miniature, page-turned weekly by conservator Frère Anselme Vaudreuil.

pages.title: Visit — Hours, Admission & Directions — The Cloister Museum
pages.content_brief: Practical visitor information. Hours: Tuesday–Sunday, 10h00–17h30; closed Mondays and on the Solemnity of All Saints. Admission: 14 € adult, 9 € student or pilgrim, free to children under 12 and to all visitors on the first Sunday of every month. Address: 7 rue des Vitraux, 77300 Fontainebleau. Telephone: +33 1 64 22 41 18. Wheelchair access through the north transept entrance; an audio guide is available in French, English, German, and Latin.

pages.title: Lectures, Vespers Concerts & Education — The Cloister Museum
pages.content_brief: A calendar of upcoming programs. The Michaelmas Lecture, 'Plate Tracery and the Geometry of the Quatrefoil,' delivered by Dr. Hélène Marquand of the Sorbonne, 14 November at 19h00. Vespers Concerts in the Lancet Hall: the ensemble Schola Sancti Dionysii sings Léonin and Pérotin organum every second Friday by candlelight. Children's programs include 'A Mason's Apprenticeship' (ages 8–12, Saturdays) and the autumn Scriptorium workshop in gold-leaf gilding for adults.

pages.title: About the Museum & History of the Cloister — The Cloister Museum
pages.content_brief: History of the institution. Founded in 1897 by the antiquarian Édouard de Saint-Pierre on the grounds of a dissolved Cistercian priory, the museum was reorganized in 1923 around the donation of the de Saint-Pierre stained-glass collection. The current cloister and lancet hall were rebuilt 1956–1962 to designs by the architect Auguste Perret's atelier following war damage. Lists the curatorial staff, the Board of Trustees chaired by the Comte Henri de Vauclair, and acknowledges founding patrons of the new Rose Window Study wing.
